clue.text: The entertainment of guests could be up to her, say

definitions.text: The entertainment of guests could be up to her, say

parts.words: The entertainment of guests could be up to her, say
parts.note: a gathering of visitors staying at someone's home, whose running is left to the hostess of that home

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is one cryptic description: the entertaining of visitors, which in a big country home might well be left to the hostess.
explanation.definitionFit: A gathering of guests staying for days at a country home is a classic form of hospitality, organised by the lady of the house.

clue.text: Nag a drudge

definitions.meaning: a nag is a tired old horse
a drudge is someone who does dull ...-work

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a worn-out horse for hire and a writer or worker grinding out routine labour.

clue.text: 'ave a look for a girl in fiction

indicators.note: the dropped letter in 'ave shows a Cockney speaker, so the next word loses its opening aitch too

parts.note: to have a look for something is to hunt for it
Ruth is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Someone told to look for a girl in a novel, in Cockney accents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ave (have, minus its H) signals a Cockney dropping aitches, so HUNT becomes 'UNT.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiction in the sense of something made up is a falsehood or lie.

clue.text: Next, a hair oil that can produce a lift

indicators.note: these words say the letters of the preceding words can be worked into something new

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An advert: next, a hair tonic that gives your hair lift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lift' looks like body in hair from a hair product; it means a rise in spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: A lift in mood is a feeling of elation and high spirits.

clue.text: I had to stress outside chance

indicators.note: outside says the word for stress goes around the letters for I had

parts.note: an accent is the stress laid on a syllable
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: Someone stressing that something lay outside their control.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens by chance, unplanned, is a mishap or fluke.

clue.text: Put a roof on yonder church

parts.note: yonder means that one over there

explanation.surface: An instruction to re-roof the church over there.
explanation.definitionFit: To cover a building's top with straw or reeds is to give it a roof.

clue.text: Provided on return with quiet perch, perhaps

indicators.note: on return says the word for provided is read backwards

parts.note: if means provided that
SH is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: Someone, on coming back, is given a quiet place to sit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perch' reads as a resting place but is a freshwater species; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The perch is a freshwater species, one example of a creature that swims.

clue.text: Fashionable lady of the Crossways in a state

parts.note: in means fashionable
Diana of the Crossways is a novel by George Meredith, its heroine Diana

explanation.surface: A stylish heroine from a Victorian novel finds herself in an agitated condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a state' reads as agitated; 'in' is a link and 'a state' the definition, a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: This is one of the fifty states of the USA, in the Midwest.

clue.text: River's got fish — about 12

parts.note: the Humber is the river estuary in north-east England; with the 's it gives an S
the ide is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A river has got some fish, about a dozen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about 12' reads as a count of fish, but refers to 12-across, HULL: Humberside was the English county surrounding that city.
explanation.definitionFit: The former county formed in 1974 surrounded the port city at 12, so it lies around it.

clue.text: A fisherman likes to, but not while sweeping

definitions.text: A fisherman likes to, but not while sweeping

parts.words: A fisherman likes to, but not while sweeping
parts.note: an angler is happy to land a shellfish, but sweeping is rowing with one long oar, where the same phrase means fouling the stroke

explanation.walkthrough: A sweep is a long oar, so 'sweeping' means rowing: the oarsman's fault shares its name with landing a shellfish.
explanation.definitionFit: In rowing, the phrase means a blade caught in the water so the rower is jerked back; literally an angler's prize.

clue.text: A mother? He never had one

parts.note: a dam is an animal's mother

explanation.surface: A question about motherhood, answered by the one man who had no mother.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition refers back to 'A mother': the first man, created rather than born, never had one.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the first man was formed from dust, so had no mother.

clue.text: Low character, this old soldier

parts.note: David Low was a cartoonist whose pompous retired army officer became a famous figure

explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks like base or vulgar, but is the cartoonist David Low of the London Evening Standard.
explanation.definitionFit: The cartoonist David Low created this blustering reactionary ex-officer, whose name became a byword for diehard conservatism.

clue.text: Prepare strawberries in port

definitions.meaning: to pull the green calyx off strawberries before eating
the Yorkshire port on the Humber estuary

explanation.definitionFit: The word means removing the leafy tops from soft fruit and is also a major east-coast English seaport.

clue.text: 6 about to deserve degree

indicators.note: about says the word for the fish is turned round

parts.note: 6-across is FISH, and cod is one example
to rate is to merit or deserve

explanation.surface: A candidate about to earn an academic qualification.
explanation.walkthrough: '6' points to 6-across (a fish, here COD); 'about' turns it to DOC.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest university award, a PhD, is a research qualification.

clue.text: Mr Sprat, a capital writer

parts.note: Jack Sprat is the nursery-rhyme man who could eat no fat
London is the capital of the UK

explanation.surface: A nursery-rhyme man who writes very well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' looks like the adjective meaning excellent, but is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: The American author of The Call of the Wild was a novelist and short-story writer.

clue.text: A fan here and there rioting .

annotationWithheld.why: A fan here and there rioting ... (8): ADHERENT is HERE AND THERE rearranged less HERE, so 'here' is both in the fodder and the letters removed, one word doing two jobs; no other parse found
annotationWithheld.clue: A fan here and there rioting .

clue.text: … or lost in the crowd, in Slough

indicators.note: lost in says the little word is buried inside the word for a crowd

parts.note: a mass is a large crowd
taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing the fan: or swallowed up by the crowd in a Berkshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough looks like the Berkshire town, but here means a bog. The ellipsis joins this clue to the one before only for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A slough is a swamp or bog, and figuratively a hopeless mess.

clue.text: We agree to listen more than once

indicators.note: more than once says the word is written twice

parts.note: to hear is to listen

explanation.surface: We agree to listen several times.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated call is how members of Parliament or an audience voice agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: The doubled cry is a traditional expression of approval and assent at meetings.

clue.text: Shrew packs a right in unarmed combat

indicators.note: packs says the shrew holds the next letters inside her

parts.note: Kate is the title shrew of Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew

explanation.surface: A shrewish woman packs a right hook in a fist fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrew' reads as a scold, but is Shakespeare's Katherina (Kate).
explanation.definitionFit: This Japanese martial art is fighting with hands and feet rather than weapons.

clue.text: The umpire has to impose control verbally — what a burden!

parts.note: ref is short for referee, an umpire

indicators.note: verbally says the word for control is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: to rein in is to impose control

explanation.surface: The umpire must lay down the law out loud, what a load to carry!
explanation.walkthrough: 'burden' looks like a load; it is the old word for a song's chorus.
explanation.definitionFit: A burden, in old usage, is the chorus or repeated lines of a song.

clue.text: Rose and roared again?

definitions.meaning: bell is the roar of a rutting stag, so this is belled once more

explanation.definitionFit: The word means rose in revolt and, split up, bellowed for a second time, as a stag does.

clue.text: King's almost without a student

parts.note: Lear is Shakespeare's king

indicators.note: without says a letter is taken away

parts.note: near means almost

explanation.surface: The king nearly lacks a pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil or trainee is someone still acquiring knowledge.

clue.text: Not fixed in Alabama port

definitions.meaning: the Gulf of Mexico seaport in Alabama

explanation.definitionFit: The word means movable and is also the name of a seaport on the Gulf coast of Alabama.

clue.text: Sick of dividing 11 into four

indicators.note: dividing says the abbreviation splits the number word apart

parts.note: 11-down is COLONEL BLIMP, and COL is the abbreviation of colonel

explanation.surface: Someone sickened by dividing eleven by four.
explanation.walkthrough: '11' points to 11-down, the colonel, abbreviated as usual in army ranks; 'dividing' looks like arithmetic but means splitting the number word.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling a bit unwell or below par is the idiom's meaning.

clue.text: Suffer in Paddington, for instance

definitions.meaning: to put up with or endure
Paddington is the marmalade-loving ... of children's books

explanation.definitionFit: The word means to tolerate or endure, and Paddington is a fictional bear from Peru.

clue.text: Dressed many a boy

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, many
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A lot of boys get clothes on.
explanation.definitionFit: Clad is an old word for wearing clothes, as in clothed.

clue.text: Lottery providing minor return

indicators.note: return says the word for minor is read backwards

parts.note: a ward is a minor in the care of a guardian

explanation.surface: A lottery offering a small payback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minor return' reads as a small payout but means the word for a minor goes backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A raffle or prize draw is a lottery.

clue.text: Pips possibly obtained from giant limes

indicators.note: obtained from says the answer is got by reworking the letters of the next words

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fruit seeds got from huge citrus fruits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pips' looks like fruit seeds; it means the short radio beeps (the Greenwich pips) marking the hour on BBC radio.
explanation.definitionFit: The six short beeps broadcast by the BBC at the hour are an audible marker of the exact hour.

clue.text: Sisters in unsisterly displays

indicators.note: displays says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Sisters behaving in an unsisterly way.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of a female religious order are addressed as Sister.

clue.text: Scouts should always show willing

definitions.meaning: the Scout movement's motto tells members to be ready at all times
to be ready and willing to act

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the Scouts' motto and also means being ready for whatever comes.
